title: Matter & Its Changes
description: Grade 4 Science: matter and its changes — states of matter, melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, dissolving, and reversible vs irreversible changes. Interactive sim included.

topics.title: The Three States of Matter
topics.concept:
Everything around us is matter, and matter is found in three states:

  • 🧊 Solids keep their own shape (ice, wood, stone).
  • 💧 Liquids flow and take the shape of their container (water, milk).
  • 💨 Gases spread out to fill all the space (air, steam).

Tiny invisible pieces called particles make up all matter. In a solid they are packed tight; in a liquid they are looser; in a gas they spread far apart.

recap: Matter has three states: solid, liquid and gas.
Solids keep shape; liquids flow; gases spread out.
Tiny particles are packed tight in solids and far apart in gases.

wonder.text: Ice, water and steam look so different — yet all three are the same water. How can one thing wear three different costumes?

qa.q: Why does a solid keep its shape but a gas does not?
qa.a: In a solid, the tiny particles are packed tightly and cannot move much, so it keeps its shape. In a gas, particles are far apart and move freely, so a gas spreads out everywhere.

qa.q: Is steam really the same as ice?
qa.a: Yes! Ice, liquid water and steam are all made of the very same water — just with the particles packed differently. Heat or cold changes which state it is in.

topics.title: Melting and Freezing
topics.concept:
Heating and cooling can change matter from one state to another:

  • 🔥 Melting — heat changes a SOLID into a LIQUID (ice → water, butter melts).
  • ❄️ Freezing — cooling changes a LIQUID into a SOLID (water → ice).

Melting and freezing are opposites. The same thing can melt and freeze again and again!

recap: Melting: heat changes a solid into a liquid.
Freezing: cooling changes a liquid into a solid.
Melting and freezing are opposite changes.

wonder.text: Leave an ice cream in the sun and it turns runny. Put water in the freezer and it turns hard. What is happening?

qa.q: Do all solids melt at the same heat?
qa.a: No! Ice melts in gentle warmth, but chocolate melts a bit slower, and metal needs a huge amount of heat to melt. Different solids melt at different temperatures.

qa.q: Is freezing the opposite of melting?
qa.a: Yes! Melting turns a solid into a liquid with heat; freezing turns a liquid into a solid with cold. They are opposite changes.

topics.title: Evaporation and Condensation
topics.concept:
Water can change between liquid and gas too:

  • ☀️ Evaporation — heat changes a LIQUID into a GAS (water → water vapour). This dries wet clothes.
  • ☁️ Condensation — cooling changes a GAS back into a LIQUID (vapour → water drops). This makes a cold bottle wet outside.
topics.visual: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="300" height="150" fill="#eef9ff"/><text x="70" y="80" font-size="44" text-anchor="middle">💧</text><defs><marker id="m2a" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="4" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L9 4 L0 8 z" fill="#FFC93C"/></marker></defs><defs><marker id="m2b" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="4" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L9 4 L0 8 z" fill="#5aa0e0"/></marker></defs><g stroke="#FFC93C" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#m2a)"><line x1="108" y1="64" x2="186" y2="64"/></g><text x="147" y="56" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#caa017" text-anchor="middle">heat</text><g stroke="#5aa0e0" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#m2b)"><line x1="186" y1="92" x2="108" y2="92"/></g><text x="147" y="110" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#1f7fe0" text-anchor="middle">cool</text><text x="215" y="80" font-size="40" text-anchor="middle">☁️</text><text x="150" y="135" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#1f7fe0" text-anchor="middle">Evaporation & Condensation</text></svg>
recap: Evaporation: heat turns a liquid into a gas.
Condensation: cooling turns a gas back into a liquid.
They are opposite changes, like melting and freezing.

wonder.text: A wet floor dries up, and a cold bottle gets wet outside. Where does the water go — and come from?

qa.q: Why do wet clothes dry faster in the sun?
qa.a: The Sun's heat speeds up evaporation, turning the water in the clothes into vapour quickly. More heat and breeze mean faster drying.

qa.q: Why does a cold glass 'sweat' on a hot day?
qa.a: Warm water vapour in the air touches the cold glass, cools down, and condenses into tiny water drops on the outside. That is condensation.

topics.title: Mixing and Dissolving
topics.concept:
When we mix things into water, two things can happen:

  • 🍚 Some things dissolve — they mix in completely and seem to disappear (sugar, salt, coffee). The water becomes a clear mixture called a solution.
  • 🏖️ Some things do not dissolve — they stay separate and sink or float (sand, oil, chalk).

Things dissolve faster in WARM water and when we STIR.

recap: Some things dissolve in water (sugar, salt) and seem to vanish.
Some do not dissolve (sand, oil) and stay separate.
Warm water and stirring make things dissolve faster.

wonder.text: Stir sugar into water and it seems to vanish. Stir in sand and it just sinks. What is the difference?

qa.q: If sugar disappears in water, is it gone?
qa.a: No — it is still there, just broken into pieces too tiny to see, spread through the water. Taste it and the water is sweet! That is dissolving.

qa.q: How can I make sugar dissolve faster?
qa.a: Use warm water and stir it! Heat and stirring help the sugar break apart and mix into the water much more quickly.

topics.title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes
topics.concept:
Changes in matter come in two kinds:

  • 🔄 Reversible changes can be undone — you get the original thing back. (Melting ice, freezing water, dissolving sugar.)
  • ➡️ Irreversible changes cannot be undone — a brand new thing is made. (Cooking an egg, burning paper, baking a cake.)
topics.visual: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect width="320" height="150" fill="#fff"/><text x="60" y="70" font-size="36" text-anchor="middle">🧊</text><text x="60" y="96" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="22" font-weight="700" fill="#16a06a" text-anchor="middle">↔</text><text x="60" y="130" font-size="30" text-anchor="middle">💧</text><text x="60" y="148" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#16a06a" text-anchor="middle">Reversible</text><line x1="160" y1="20" x2="160" y2="140" stroke="#e0e0e0" stroke-width="2"/><text x="250" y="70" font-size="34" text-anchor="middle">🥚</text><defs><marker id="m4" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="4" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L9 4 L0 8 z" fill="#c0392b"/></marker></defs><g stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#m4)"><line x1="230" y1="92" x2="270" y2="92"/></g><text x="250" y="128" font-size="30" text-anchor="middle">🍳</text><text x="250" y="148" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#c0392b" text-anchor="middle">Irreversible</text></svg>
recap: Reversible changes can be undone (melting, freezing, dissolving).
Irreversible changes make a new thing (cooking, burning).
Cooking an egg cannot be undone.

wonder.text: Melted ice can become ice again — but a fried egg can never become raw. Why can some changes undo, but not others?

qa.q: Why can't a cooked egg become raw again?
qa.a: Cooking changes the egg into something completely new — there is no way to turn it back. That makes cooking an irreversible change.
Yes! Melted chocolate can be cooled to become solid chocolate again. Only the shape changed, not what it is made of — so it is reversible.

questions.q: Matter is found in how many states?
questions.explanation: Matter has three states: solid, liquid and gas.
Melting uses heat to turn a solid into a liquid.
Freezing uses cold to turn a liquid into a solid.
Sugar dissolves in water; sand and oil do not.

questions.q: A change that CANNOT be undone is…
questions.explanation: An irreversible change makes a new thing and cannot be undone.
Burnt paper becomes ash and cannot become paper again — irreversible.

questions.q: Why does a gas spread out to fill a room?
options: Its particles are far apart and move freely
questions.explanation: In a gas, particles are far apart and move freely, so it spreads everywhere.

questions.q: If sugar 'disappears' in water, where is it?
options: Broken into tiny pieces spread through the water
questions.explanation: The sugar is still there as tiny pieces spread through the water — the water tastes sweet.

questions.q: How can you make sugar dissolve faster?
options: Use cold water and don't stir
questions.explanation: Warm water and stirring make sugar dissolve faster.

questions.q: Why is melting chocolate a reversible change?
options: It can be cooled back into solid chocolate
questions.explanation: Cooled melted chocolate becomes solid chocolate again — only the shape changed.
Evaporation turns liquid to gas; condensation turns gas back to liquid — opposites.
